details:
**Vientiane and Phnom Penh**
Two national capitals on the Mekong: Vientiane, the capital of Laos, and Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. They appear in almost every question, usually near the end.

**Tonle Sap reversal**
The Tonle Sap is a large lake in Cambodia linked to the Mekong at Phnom Penh by the Tonle Sap River. During the monsoon floods the Mekong pushes water up the river into the lake, which swells greatly. When the rainy season ends the flow reverses, and the lake drains back into the Mekong, replenishing it. The flow changes direction twice a year.

**Mekong Delta and the South China Sea**
After Phnom Penh the river splits into several branches and forms a huge delta in southern Vietnam, near Ho Chi Minh City, before emptying into the South China Sea. The Vietnamese call it Cửu Long, "Nine Dragons." The delta is famous for the floating markets of Can Tho and for farming basa catfish. The ancient Kingdom of Funan dug canals there in the early centuries CE.

**Khone Falls and the 4,000 Islands**
Khone Phapheng Falls in southern Laos is the widest waterfall in the world. It blocks navigation and stopped French colonial plans to use the river as a trade route into China. Just upstream is Si Phan Don, the "4,000 Islands," a maze of islands and channels below the city of Pakse.

**Mekong giant catfish**
One of the largest freshwater fish in the world, now critically endangered, and named for the river. A large population survives in the Tonle Sap. Dams threaten its migrations, and the Xayaburi Dam in Laos was designed with fish passages ("fish elevators") partly to protect it.

**Golden Triangle and the Ruak River**
The Ruak River meets the Mekong where Thailand, Laos, and Myanmar come together. This area, the Golden Triangle, was historically one of the world's largest opium- and drug-producing regions.

**Laos–Thailand border**
For long stretches the Mekong forms the border between Laos and Thailand. Several Thai–Lao Friendship Bridges cross it there. Its Thai and Lao name, Mae Nam Khong, is often explained as "Mother of Waters."

**Luang Prabang**
The former royal capital of Laos, a UNESCO World Heritage site full of Buddhist monasteries, at the confluence of the Mekong and the Nam Khan. Kaipen, sheets of dried river algae gathered and sold by local women, is a well-known specialty there.

**Naga fireballs**
Glowing balls that are said to rise silently from the river in late October, especially near Nong Khai in Thailand, across from Vientiane. Locals credit them to the mythical serpent Naga. One proposed scientific explanation is gas released from the riverbed, such as phosphine, but none has been confirmed.

**Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan (Lancang)**
The Mekong begins on the Tibetan Plateau in Zadoi County, Qinghai. In China it is called the Lancang. In the Hengduan Mountains of Yunnan it runs side by side with the Salween to the west and the Yangtze to the east, forming the Three Parallel Rivers UNESCO site, with the Mekong as the middle river.

**Manwan Dam, Xayaburi Dam, and the Mekong River Commission**
The Manwan Dam in Yunnan, finished in the early 1990s, was the first dam on the main river, and many more have been built or planned since. The Mekong River Commission, an intergovernmental body of the downstream countries, coordinates management of the river and has raised concerns about these dams. Many dams have also been built on tributaries such as the Sesan and Nam Ou.

**Khorat Plateau and the Mun and Chi rivers**
The Khorat Plateau covers northeastern Thailand (Isan). The Chi River joins the Mun, and the Mun empties into the Mekong, draining the plateau.

**Pakse and Champasak**
Pakse is a major city in southern Laos at the junction of the Mekong and the Xe Don River. It was the capital of the former Kingdom of Champasak.

**French Mekong Expedition (Doudart de Lagrée and Francis Garnier)**
The French expedition of 1866–1868, led by Ernest Doudart de Lagrée and later by Francis Garnier, made the first systematic map of the river. It found that rapids and falls made the Mekong useless as a trade route into China.

**Giant freshwater stingray (Boramy) and Wonders of the Mekong**
In 2022 a roughly 300-kilogram (661-pound) giant freshwater stingray was caught in Cambodia, the largest freshwater fish ever recorded. The research project Wonders of the Mekong tagged it, named it Boramy, and released it. The river has more giant fish species than any other, including the giant barb Probarbus.
